title: Stone ground vs machine ground spices: what changes in the grinding
summary: How high-speed mills and slow stone mills turn whole spices into powder, why heat matters for aroma, and how HariLeaf grinds its turmeric and chillies.
body:
Ground spices start as whole, dried roots, pods or seeds. How they are turned into powder affects the colour, the aroma and the texture you get in the pack.

## Machine grinding

Most spice powder is made in high-speed mills — hammer, pin or pulveriser mills — that break the spice by impact at very high speed. They are fast and grind a lot of spice per hour. The friction warms the powder as it is ground; some mills cool the grinding chamber to limit this.

## Stone grinding

A stone mill turns slowly, crushing and shearing the spice between two stones. It grinds much less per hour, so it is done in small lots. Grinding slowly produces less heat.

## Why heat matters

Much of what you smell when you open a pack of ground spice comes from volatile oils, which evaporate more readily when warm. That is why we grind slowly: slow grinding runs cooler than high-speed milling, which is how more of the aroma and colour stays in the powder.

## How HariLeaf makes its spice powders

Our turmeric and chillies are dried whole in the sun, then ground slowly on stone in small lots. Every pack carries its batch code and packed-on date, and lab results appear on the product page as they come in. Read more about [how we grow, mill and grind](/our-process/).

## Buying and storing ground spices

- Check the packed-on date: ground spices lose aroma over the months after grinding.
- Keep them in an airtight container, away from light, heat and moisture.
- Buy packs you will use within a few months rather than a large stock.

Try [haldi doodh](/recipes/haldi-doodh/) or [Konkan-style masoor khichdi](/recipes/konkan-masoor-khichdi/), or [see our spices](/spices/).
